title: Humboldt and Bonpland in the Spanish Americas
intro: Alexander von Humboldt and the French botanist Aimé Bonpland sailed to Spain's American realms in 1799 with authorisation from the Spanish crown and Humboldt's own funds. They travelled through Venezuela, Cuba, the Andes and New Spain, and returned by way of the United States.
ending: Humboldt set sail for Europe from the mouth of the Delaware and landed at Bordeaux on 3 August 1804. He spent the next two decades publishing the results, and the work made his name in scientific circles.

stops.text: Humboldt and Bonpland, armed with the King of Spain's authorisation, sailed from La Coruña on the ship Pizarro.
stops.quote: Armed with authorization from the King of Spain, Humboldt and Bonpland made haste to sail, taking the ship Pizarro from La Coruña, on 5 June 1799.

stops.text: The Pizarro stopped for six days on Tenerife, and Humboldt climbed the volcano Teide.
stops.quote: The ship stopped six days on the island of Tenerife, where Humboldt climbed the volcano Teide

stops.text: The Pizarro landed at Cumaná. An outbreak of typhoid on board had made the captain change course from Havana to northern South America.
stops.quote: then sailed on to the New World, landing at Cumaná, Venezuela, on 16 July.

stops.text: At the invitation of the captain general, Manuel de Guevara y Vasconcelos, Humboldt stayed in Caracas for about two months. He then began his researches in the valley of Aragua.
stops.quote: At the invitation of the captain general, Manuel de Guevara y Vasconcelos, Humboldt stayed in Caracas for about two months, leaving in February.

stops.text: Humboldt visited the mission at Caripe and explored the Guácharo cavern, where he found the oilbird, which he made known to science as Steatornis caripensis.
stops.quote: Humboldt visited the mission at Caripe and explored the Guácharo cavern, where he found the oilbird, which he was to make known to science as Steatornis caripensis.

stops.text: They sailed from Venezuela on 24 November 1800 and landed in Cuba on 19 December. In Havana Humboldt surveyed the city and the nearby towns, and met the plant collector John Fraser.
stops.quote: On 24 November 1800, the two friends set sail for Cuba, landing on 19 December, where they met fellow botanist and plant collector John Fraser.

stops.text: From Cartagena de Indias they went up the swollen Magdalena River to Honda and reached Bogotá. There they met José Celestino Mutis and stayed until 8 September 1801.
stops.quote: Ascending the swollen stream of the Magdalena River to Honda, they arrived in Bogotá on 6 July 1801, where they met the Spanish botanist José Celestino Mutis

stops.text: Humboldt and Bonpland crossed the frozen ridges of the Cordillera Real on a tedious and difficult journey and reached Quito. They hoped to meet the French expedition of Baudin.
stops.quote: They crossed the frozen ridges of the Cordillera Real and reached Quito on 6 January 1802, after a tedious and difficult journey.

stops.text: Humboldt, Bonpland, Carlos Montúfar and a number of Indians climbed the extinct volcano Chimborazo to 19,286 feet (5,878 m), a record for a westerner, about 1,000 feet short of the summit.
stops.quote: their climb of the extinct, snow-capped volcano Chimborazo, where Humboldt and his party, consisting of himself, Bonpland, a number of Indians and the Ecuadorian nobleman Carlos Montúfar, reached an altitude of 19,286 feet (5,878 m).

stops.text: At Callao, the main port for Peru, Humboldt observed the transit of Mercury on 9 November and studied guano, whose later introduction into Europe was due mainly to his writings.
stops.quote: At Callao, the main port for Peru, Humboldt observed the transit of Mercury on 9 November and studied the fertilizing properties of guano

stops.text: Unable to join a voyage to the Pacific, they left Guayaquil and landed at Acapulco. Humboldt surveyed the bay to fix its longitude, as the ship's captain had reckoned it wrongly.
stops.quote: Humboldt and Bonpland landed in Acapulco on 15 February 1803, and from there they went to Taxco, a silver-mining town in modern Guerrero.

stops.text: From Acapulco they went to Taxco, a silver-mining town in modern Guerrero. The route was suitable only for mule trains, and Humboldt measured elevations all along it.
stops.quote: and from there they went to Taxco, a silver-mining town in modern Guerrero.

stops.text: Humboldt visited Cuernavaca and, impressed by its climate, nicknamed it the City of Eternal Spring.
stops.quote: In April 1803, he visited Cuernavaca, Morelos. Impressed by its climate, he nicknamed the city the City of Eternal Spring.

stops.text: Welcomed by a letter from Viceroy José de Iturrigaray, Humboldt received a special passport and access to crown records, mines and estates. He found it the largest city in the Americas.
stops.quote: Humboldt and Bonpland arrived in Mexico City, having been officially welcomed via a letter from the king's representative in New Spain, Viceroy Don José de Iturrigaray.

stops.text: Humboldt spent time at the Valenciana silver mine, then the most important in the Spanish empire. He studied the whole mining complex and its output statistics.
stops.quote: Humboldt spent time at the Valenciana silver mine in Guanajuato, central New Spain, at the time the most important in the Spanish empire.

stops.text: Humboldt left New Spain from the port of Veracruz, taking elevation measurements on the road from Mexico City. He reached Cuba on 7 January 1804 and stayed until 29 April 1804.
stops.quote: Humboldt and Bonpland stopped again in Cuba, leaving from the port of Veracruz and arriving in Cuba on 7 January 1804, staying until 29 April 1804.

stops.text: Leaving Cuba, Humboldt made an unplanned visit to the United States. In Philadelphia he met Caspar Wistar, Benjamin Smith Barton and Benjamin Rush.
stops.quote: Arriving in Philadelphia, which was a center of learning in the U.S., Humboldt met with some of the major scientific figures of the era

stops.text: Humboldt held long discussions with President Thomas Jefferson on science and on New Spain, and wrote him a two-page report on where the border of Louisiana lay.
stops.quote: After arriving in Washington D.C, Humboldt held numerous intense discussions with Jefferson on both scientific matters and also his year-long stay in New Spain.

stops.text: After six weeks in the United States, Humboldt set sail from the mouth of the Delaware and landed at Bordeaux.
stops.quote: After six weeks, Humboldt set sail for Europe from the mouth of the Delaware and landed at Bordeaux on 3 August 1804.

notes: The article is a biography; this is the 1799-1804 expedition only. Left out: the Orinoco and Casiquiare trip (only rivers, no town or mission named; Lake Valencia, the Guanoco lake and Avila mount named in passing), Cartagena de Indias and Honda (folded into Bogotá's text), Pichincha, Lima (only 'en route for Lima'), Guayaquil (folded into Acapulco's text), the second stay in Cuba (no town named, folded into Veracruz). Dates are null only where the article gives none. Doubtful: Callao '9 November' has no year in the article; 1802 is taken from the section (Quito, 6 January 1802, is the nearest year before it). Caracas 'February 1800' is the month of leaving (the article gives 'leaving in February' after the 1799 arrival and before the Orinoco trip of February 1800). Havana: the 1800 year follows from the 24 November 1800 sailing. Taxco has no date of its own and repeats part of the Acapulco quotation. Caripe: wp is the Venezuelan town.
